title: A divided South Africa needs Arendt
subtitle: Polarising politics needs Hannah Arendt
author: Thiven Reddy
introduction: The South African elections have exposed a political world characterised by a saturation of noisy opinion and a lack of ethics. But, Thiven Reddy writes, there is a way through this without reverting to the divisive authoritarian politics of South Africa’s history. Hannah Arendt reminds us that the ancient Greek marriage of philosophy and politics can create a better, more inclusive society.
body:
In a time of potential dramatic change in South Africa, the death of Socrates provides us with a model of dialogue, friendship, and politics that can help us navigate the problems of civic society. A key theme surrounding modern electoral politics – think US elections and Trump, or currently in South Africa – is opinion and its consequences. Drawing from a reading of Hannah Arendt, I want to make the case that politics is nothing without opinion. Yet, even though opinion is necessary in politics, we must emphasize the ancient Greek argument that politics driven exclusively by opinion suppresses the role of personal ethics and conscience, which in turn represses the political will to find the good life. A philosophical approach to political opinion can orient it away from harm towards the public good.

This ancient Greek conclusion helps us to bridge an impasse of division and politics in a country grappling with its settler colonial history and corrupt dominant party politics. The South African elections and the emerging political culture in the country openly expose the relationship of opinion to knowledge – or the separation of politics and philosophy. I will refer to an article by Arendt to discuss the relationship of elections to 'rules of a political system' and highlight the differences between Plato and Aristotle to the death of Socrates, concerning the use of dialectically understood knowledge. This debate over the role of opinion and dialectical knowledge exposes us to the limits of politics in the ‘extreme case’ of a society like South Africa. This is pulled into stark focus by a spectrum of historically inherited inequalities and the questionable values of its political class, in contrast to the alienated majority living in squalor.

In transitional societies, many features of the political terrain, including the rules of the political system, remain unsettled, taking generations to consolidate. One factor here has to do with the length or period of existence of the rules under which politics is practiced: the older the political system, the more stable the rules, the younger the political system, the more unsettled the rules.

The ruling party since 1994 promoted in particular the claim that democratic South Africa was the outcome of revolution rather than negotiations.

Societies face particular challenges when the political system must confront issues where most values are divisive, and most issues strongly debated. Everyone is an expert on every issue, opinion matters, and this creates a densely congested world of opinion. This is a not-so-unexpected outcome where subjects feel legally recognized as citizens for the first time. In South Africa very few issues or values are not the purview of politics: everything is or potentially politicized, and elections operate as ceremonial moments, formalizing collective attitudes to change and ritual practices of national belonging through citizen consent. In May 2024, South Africans will participate in the country’s seventh national election.

The South African constitution sets out the rules of its political system. It also points to the transition from authoritarian Apartheid in the 1990s, revealing three centuries of settler colonial relations that characterized the society. It is important to note that the ‘rules’ of South Africa’s political system are the product of negotiation. As a society in transition, the political system and its rules in South Africa remain the subject of ideological battles surrounding democratic politics.

The South African democratic political system emerged from a long history of racial division and conflict, the outcomes of popular mobilization and an end to a Cold War global situation has paved the way to a negotiated constitution and a reconstituted political community. Currently, none of the key actors will honestly admit to the other that the constitution was ‘negotiated.’ Each prefers to claim that it ‘won’ the war and to ideologically mobilize supporters behind such beliefs.  The ruling party since 1994 promoted in particular the claim that democratic South Africa was the outcome of revolution rather than negotiations. This insistence upon the narrative of ‘winning the revolution’ obscures the compromises at the heart of the South Africa transition.

Yet the South African political system shares features from the two broad political frameworks to emerge from a Western tradition of liberal democratic influences: the English-rooted majoritarian and American-influenced federalist. In addition, there are consensual features drawn from proportional systems. The challenge will for some time be the tension between the rules of the political system and the political culture drawn from a history of conflict over racial nationalisms. Further complicating this situation is the historical division between the political elites and the mass of subaltern citizens, where political elites under democracy control access to the state and build upon available and historical opportunistic relations with emerging and established capital.

SUGGESTED READING Trump vs Biden: It doesn't matter By Marcus Papadopoulos

Another key tension feeding into this background and evident in South African democratic elections is the prevalence of opinion and ‘tested’ worldly knowledge. This is where Arendt can help us clarify the problem and the value of opinion in the body politic. Arendt wrote that Socrates in ancient Greece understood opinion to be a personal view describing how the ‘world reveals itself to me.’ Consequently, it led to where as a value ‘standards and measures’ disappear – an ideological notion pervasive in South African society where mechanical, bureaucratic-inspired transformation assumes the primary imperative. Opinion or doxa also meant 'fame,' or ‘search for splendor,’ and we can witness, again from South African experience, how in its key institutions in state and civil society post 1994, self-promotion and standing out among the like-minded became prominent.

Socrates understood the world of knowledge and ultimately ‘truth-searching’ as an argumentative dialogue, a dialectic of contested opposing views such that the competitively most convincing idea prevails yet remains always open to question and verification. This is a challenge no society can avoid taking seriously – if convincingly argued, non-contradictory discourse is not sufficiently valued, there is a harsh price to pay. This old tension, Arendt reminds us, goes back to the very beginnings of writings in the Western tradition about politics and philosophy.

We may have heard it said that every person is a philosopher. Some may find this a strange claim to make, but it is also enriched by its very opposite claim that people – and the reference is usually to ‘the masses’ – lack the reason to develop proper knowledge, which is always going to be the preserve of the few who stand out amongst their peers in the quality of their logic and argumentation.

Without these debates concerning Socrates, South Africa’s constitutional arrangement would arguably look fundamentally different.

The assumption is that all ideas are not equal, just like one champion stands out amongst 100-meter sprint competitors, or one or a few amongst mathematicians or sociological theories.  This view in the history of ideas had a strong influence on politics and especially democratic politics:  ‘the people’ were essentially idiots, lacked wisdom, education, and good sense, and therefore should not be given the responsibility to determine societal outcomes for the entire polity.  Even if this view was not entirely nor uncritically embraced, it still impacted various versions of representative democracy, including parliamentary models.

Arendt traces a significant lesson for the relationship between philosophy and politics to the killing of the wise old thinker and teacher, Socrates. The debates elicited by the death of Socrates had a profound impact on how we think in contemporary political discourse about the responsibilities of citizens, decisions, and rights of voting, elections, and their consequences.

Without these debates concerning Socrates, South Africa’s constitutional arrangement would arguably look fundamentally different. In contrast to the ‘men of action,’ the politicians who dominate politics, Socrates insisted in his defense that ‘I know what I do not know,’ preaching that a wise person knows that ‘mere mortals’ cannot be wise. This is in stark contrast to the world of opinion we are all familiar with in politics and civil society. Here, each arrogantly considers his or her view the last word on the matter, a practice that characterizes South Africa’s national political elite and supporting analysts – and in recent decades an increasingly familiar value in our universities and research centers too.

Socrates was sentenced to death by the citizens of Athens – or at least the minority who qualified to vote – who found him guilty of miseducating the youth. Arendt writes of three responses to the death of Socrates. Plato draws from the death of Socrates the problems with politics, the role of the masses in it, and the dominance of unverified opinion, persuasion, and rhetoric. These, for Arendt, summarize the worst features of politics, leading to outcomes like the death of good persons and the support for, if not the celebration, of societies' unprincipled, opportunistic elements. If this opportunistic turn has come to characterize South African politics, Plato’s argument is that politics can only be redeemed if philosophers take an active role in it, dominate the polis, and ultimately rule as philosopher-kings. This would be an unpalatable, even sinister conclusion for a country with South Africa’s history of racial apartheid and alienation.

A second response comes from Arendt’s interpretation of Socrates’ practice and teaching. Socrates did not substitute universal truth and wisdom, as Plato did, for the limited views of ignorant citizens. Instead, Socrates believed that citizen opinion was necessary to politics and that humans could not avoid ‘knowing their world’ from the experience of how the world is ‘revealed to them.’ We know the world from our particular experience, and from this experience we are bound to formulate our opinions.

Rather than politics and philosophy, the quest for truth and ethics going together, politics moved towards an increasingly unethical pursuit of power and influence

The role of the philosopher in mediating knowledge is through participation. This entails honesty in identifying and interrogating the contradictions in argument, and, in citizen language, develops dialogue between friends to arrive at truth or higher-level argumentation. This creates opportunity for each citizen to be exposed to his or her contradictions. For Socrates, the activity of politics was the use of this active dialectic to arrive at non-contradictory positions. Opinion is valuable so long as it can be harnessed in a constructive public dialectic.

But, Arendt concludes, Socrates did not truly appreciate the inherent tension and contradiction between the key elements of philosophy and politics. Philosophy still has one foot in truth as eternal and universal, while politics is animated by fame, splendor, and superficial recognition. The philosopher’s view will be assumed to be just another opinion among many.

The complicated practice of negotiating between the two worlds of citizen politics and philosophy encouraged complexity. Socrates embraced the marketplace where citizen opinions flourished. He believed that a dialogue between opinion and knowledge, what he called maieutic or the ‘art of midwifery’, was made possible where these two parts of a polity meet. The philosopher nurtures opinions emerging in arguments into something closer to the truth. Opinions are a lower-order but necessary basis for more systematic understandings, and cannot be dispensed with. This means that citizen participation in the public domain is necessary and valuable.

The split between politics and philosophy, and the increasing distance between the two where politics became the preserve of opinion, shifted the focus on ideology, persuasiveness, and mobilization to obtain other instrumental desires. Ethics moved away into the preserve of philosophy – politics, almost inevitably, awaited Machiavelli’s instrumentalist reading of ‘the ends justify the means’.

SUGGESTED READING After the Third Way: the return of the state By Philip Collins

It should therefore come as a surprise that the ethically driven struggles led by nationalist elites against colonial racism, so central to anti-Apartheid campaigns, were neither willing nor able to dent the consequences of this split between philosophy and politics. Rather than politics and philosophy, the quest for truth and ethics going together, politics moved towards an increasingly unethical pursuit of power and influence while philosophy, truth, and ethics moved into the quiet of the study, a world of ideas unconcerned with public engagement. A country where political consciousness had tremendously rich roots to build upon in the ethics that drove black politics for nearly three hundred years opted, in its democratic transition, for a superficial, bureaucratic and mechanical approach to politics.

We can draw a few conclusions from this analysis of opinion and politics as argued by Arendt on early Greek philosophy: that every person has his or her opinion; that this opinion emerges from ones experience or how the world is revealed to the person; that in isolation, the opinion’s value or truth cannot be known; and that only in dialogue and discussion can these opinions move towards improvement and change. We need to be open to questions and engage our own opinions with those of others, in dialogue, discussion or dialectic.

This model of friendship as defined by Socrates serves as an inspiration for the deeply divided, antagonistic politics that determine the South African situation. This remains important, perhaps even more so, in a context of inequality or adversity, because it harnesses our capacity and willingness to conceive of politics as ‘seeing the world from the other fellow’s view,’ This remains the challenge. We should look to elections to expose the sharp differences in society and then build upon those discourses, working towards developing and consolidating interpersonal relationships of friendship. This worthy ideal is far from what we experience in modern elections, where Hobbes and Machiavelli hover as ever-present shadows over politicians and their political parties. But Socrates believed that it is only in friendship that the polity can move in a direction beneficial to all.
